title: Why A&Es Are Crowded: Beds, Discharge and What Can Be Done Now
label: 11 November 2026 · Winter Pressures
summary: MPs questioned emergency medicine leaders and health ministers about emergency department overcrowding, corridor care and winter planning. Witnesses said the system is in worse shape than last year: overcrowding, high bed occupancy and delayed discharges drive deaths and ambulance delays. The Royal College urged short-term actions (open all available beds, keep key services open longer, end recruitment freezes for flow-critical roles). Ministers accepted the scale of the problem, set out measures already under way (new measurements for corridor care, model EDs, discharge work, vaccine push) and pledged more national support, data work and an urgent care strategy coming imminently.

chapters.title: State of emergency departments
chapters.takeaway: EDs are entering winter in worse shape than last year: overcrowded, unsafe by clinician report, and linked to excess deaths.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We wanted to check how winter planning is going. Ian, is this year any different for emergency departments?

turns.speaker: Dr Ian Higginson
turns.text: I’d call it more 'preparations' than a full plan. Departments are already in big trouble: 67% of clinical leads said their EDs felt fairly or very unsafe in our October survey.

turns.speaker: Dr Ian Higginson
turns.text: Crowding is the main safety issue. A spot survey showed one in five patients in inappropriate areas. Long waits in EDs are linked to about 16,000 excess deaths in England.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is anything different this year that will help?

turns.speaker: Dr Ian Higginson
turns.text: People now agree the problem is system-wide, not just the ED. But that recognition hasn’t yet turned into the concrete actions we need to change outcomes this winter.

turns.speaker: Matthew Hopkins
turns.text: There has been a step change in recognising system responsibility—ambulance, primary care and hospitals—but many places vary in leadership and how they prioritise urgent care.

turns.speaker: Dr Gardner
turns.text: You said 67% feel unsafe. What does 'unsafe' mean in practice?

turns.speaker: Dr Ian Higginson
turns.text: It means patients being harmed because EDs are overcrowded. Clinicians end up doing traffic control rather than hands-on care; the longer waits start to drive worse outcomes.

chapters.title: Why the system is failing
chapters.takeaway: Main causes are overcrowding caused by slow patient flow, high bed occupancy, fewer open beds and staff shortages—no single 'magic bullet'.

turns.speaker: Dr Ian Higginson
turns.text: Overcrowding stems from either no alternatives to admission or no bed when admission is needed. About 10% of all hospital beds—roughly 13,000—are occupied by patients who no longer need them.

turns.speaker: Matthew Hopkins
turns.text: ICBs used to convene local partners; many have had their capacity cut and leadership churn, so system convening is weaker. That affects discharge and flow work.

turns.speaker: Andrew George
turns.text: Is there a golden bullet for delayed discharges?

turns.speaker: Dr Ian Higginson
turns.text: It's a 'wicked' problem: beds are the obvious need, but beds depend on hospitals working seven days, tackling delayed discharges, and the overall number of beds available.

turns.speaker: Matthew Hopkins
turns.text: Examples exist where systems work well and free beds, but adoption nationally is patchy. Reducing unnecessary length of stay and discharging routine cases earlier would help flow.

turns.speaker: Dr Gardner
turns.text: You mentioned mortality risk increases after five hours in ED. That’s worrying—so getting patients through quickly matters for survival, not just convenience.

chapters.title: Practical short-term fixes proposed
chapters.takeaway: Royal College suggests immediate actions hospitals and systems can take this winter; ministers accept the crisis and list national measures already under way.

turns.speaker: Dr Ian Higginson
turns.text: We recommended five fast actions: open and staff all available beds in overcrowded hospitals; stop routine rapid ambulance drop-offs unless the hospital is at highest escalation; ensure flow-critical services open longer (e.g., 12 hours daily, seven days); lift recruitment freezes in flow-critical services; prioritise staff support and security.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: When you say 'money is king', what do you mean?

turns.speaker: Dr Ian Higginson
turns.text: Hospital leaders face financial pressure and sometimes close wards to save money even when that worsens flow and safety. That trade-off is undermining patient care.

turns.speaker: Matthew Hopkins
turns.text: Ambulance trusts also need different performance measures: category 2 response times miss quality outcomes. Ambulances waiting outside EDs are a symptom of a blocked system.

turns.speaker: Karin Smyth
turns.text: I accept the system is entering winter in worse shape. The Government has set eradication of corridor care as a target, has model EDs and is investing in front-door services—but I hear the call to do more on the back door and flow.

turns.speaker: Dr Rowland
turns.text: We’ve started measuring corridor care since May and intend to eradicate it. We’re focusing now on the back door: definitions of 'no criteria to reside', model discharge pathways, and targeted rapid-improvement support for struggling providers.

turns.speaker: Dr Ian Higginson
turns.text: Measuring corridor care is useful, but the initial definition risks gaming (it omits ambulance waits and off-the-clock waiting areas). If we fixed four-hour performance and hospital occupancy, corridor care largely disappears.

chapters.title: Data, vaccination and leadership gaps
chapters.takeaway: Ministers promised better national data, more leadership support, an urgent care strategy 'very soon', and an intensified vaccination drive to reduce winter admissions.

turns.speaker: Paulette Hamilton
turns.text: The NAO said national data on flow is inadequate. Do you have the data needed to act?

turns.speaker: Dr Rowland
turns.text: We have lots of data on front-door and back-door outcomes, but granular local flow data sits at provider level. We’re trying to ensure consistent definitions and to use data to drive improvement, not just reporting.

turns.speaker: Karin Smyth
turns.text: We’re increasing national support where systems are under stress and will consider what national data should be mandated. We’ve appointed a patient experience director to improve capture of patient outcomes.

turns.speaker: Josh Fenton-Glynn
turns.text: Corridor care rose 14% since May—does that threaten the eradication target?

turns.speaker: Dr Rowland
turns.text: Early reporting can make numbers rise because of better reporting. But rise in corridor care is worrying and shows the need for urgent focus on flow.

turns.speaker: Sadik Al-Hassan
turns.text: What about flu and RSV—are vaccinations on track to reduce winter admissions?

turns.speaker: Dr Frances
turns.text: By 1 November we delivered 13.6m flu vaccines, up 300,000 from last year; school delivery is ahead of last year. Uptake varies by group; we’ve set multi-year targets to rebuild coverage and are pushing healthcare-worker uptake too.

turns.speaker: Karin Smyth
turns.text: We are not waiting for the social care review to act on discharge. The Department is working with local government on rough sleepers and other cohorts and will publish urgent care strategy imminently.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final point: the witnesses warned this is long-term and getting worse. Ministers acknowledged that and promised more data, targeted support and immediate actions—will it be enough this winter?

turns.speaker: Dr Ian Higginson
turns.text: Short-term mitigations can help, but many fixes need long-term investment and commitment: staffing, bed stock and seven-day system functioning. Emergency medicine can’t do magic; we need the system to deliver.
